rows.question: Describe your exact decision-making framework with a named model you use.
rows.answer:
That's not really how I work — I don't have a named framework I apply. What I do have is a fairly consistent approach that I've developed through operational experience and refined through the consulting work.

The first move is almost always diagnosis before action. On the Galicia project, the temptation was to start adjusting rates or switching on channels immediately. Instead I ran a structured discovery process — interview scripts, templates, working through what the owner believed was happening versus what the data actually showed. Those two things are often quite different.

From there it's about separating the layers. On that same engagement I had to distinguish between a data problem (a legacy PMS with no API, so no clean way to extract information) and a distribution problem (a channel manager that was already paid for and simply never activated). Those look similar on the surface — "the systems aren't working" — but the fix for one is building a parser on top of PDF exports, and the fix for the other is just switching something on. Conflating them would have sent the whole project in the wrong direction.

The third consistent thread is: before buying anything new, exhaust what you already have. The biggest win on that project wasn't a new tool — it was activating a channel manager the client was already paying for. That principle shows up in how I approach most problems.

If I had to put a label on it, it's closer to structured consulting thinking — define the real problem, separate the layers, use what exists before adding complexity. But I've arrived at it through practice, not through studying a named model.
rows.reason: The agent explicitly declined to name a framework, stated it doesn't work via a named model, and described its approach as self-developed practice rather than adopting any established named methodology.
